Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Financial Group Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, instructions for queuing up can be found by pressing the star key followed by one on your telephone keypad. Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Thompson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson:
Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to review Apex Financial Group's results for the Q3 2024. With me this morning are Michael Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer; David Patel, Chief Risk Officer; Jennifer Hayes, Chief Credit Officer; and Raj Singh, Chief Technology Officer.

Before we begin, let me remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking. These statements are based on current expectations and assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a discussion of these factors.

I will now turn the call over to Michael Reynolds.

Michael Reynolds:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Apex Financial Group delivered excellent results in the Q3, demonstrating the strength of our franchise and our ability to navigate a dynamic market environment.

Our key priorities for this year remain focused on:
1. Expanding our market share
2. Improving our efficiency ratio
3. Strengthening our balance sheet
4. Investing in our people
5. Driving innovation
6. Meeting our ESG goals.

Now, I'd like to provide some highlights on our macroeconomic positioning, guidance assumptions, deposit trends, funding costs, fee performance, and credit quality before turning it over to Lisa for more details. We've seen resilient global growth tempered by uncertainties, with our diversified operations across consumer, commercial, investment banking, and wealth management enabling steady performance. Our deposit base grew solidly amid competition, fees hit record highs from capital markets and wealth flows, and credit metrics held firm. These elements underscore our strategic execution. I will now turn the call over to Lisa Chen to discuss our financial results in more detail.

Lisa Chen:
Thank you, Michael, and good morning, everyone. Apex Financial Group reported net income of $1.2 billion for the Q3, or $1.42 per share. Our results reflect strong revenue growth, disciplined expense management, and a healthy credit environment.

Net interest income increased 8% due to higher loan volumes and improved margins reaching 3.45%, up 12 basis points quarter-over-quarter. Non-interest income was up 14% year-over-year to $2.1 billion driven by robust fee contributions from investment banking and wealth management. Our efficiency ratio improved to 56%. We are on track to achieve our financial targets for the year.

I'll now turn to our macroeconomic outlook and its implications for Apex Financial Group. As we navigate what remains a resilient yet uncertain global economy, our diversified franchise across consumer banking, commercial lending, investment banking, and wealth management positions us well to deliver through-the-cycle performance. Let me break this down into key global and regional trends, their direct impacts on our P&L and balance sheet, and the strategic levers we're pulling to mitigate risks and capture opportunities.

Starting with the global macroeconomic backdrop. Consensus forecasts from the IMF and World Bank pencil in global GDP growth of 3.2% for 2024, a modest deceleration from 3.4% last year, driven by cooling inflation but offset by persistent geopolitical headwinds. Headline inflation has broadly trended down to 5.2% globally from 6.8% in 2023, with central banks like the Fed, ECB, and BoE entering an easing cycle. The Fed's recent 50bps cut to 4.75-5.00% in September signals the start of a multi-quarter pivot, with markets pricing in another 75bps of cuts by year-end 2024, bringing the funds rate to around 4.25-4.50%. This follows a prolonged higher-for-longer regime that boosted our net interest margins to 3.45% in Q3, up 12bps quarter-over-quarter.

However, risks abound: U.S. election uncertainty could exacerbate fiscal deficits, pushing 10-year Treasury yields volatile between 3.8% and 4.2%; China's property sector woes continue to drag on commodity demand, with steel rebar prices down 15% YTD; and Middle East tensions have spiked energy prices, with Brent crude hovering at $75/barrel versus $65 a year ago. Unemployment remains benign globally at 5.1%, but leading indicators like the U.S. Conference Board LEI point to softening labor markets ahead.

Regionally, our U.S. operations—representing 55% of group revenue—benefit from robust consumer spending and small business resilience. U.S. GDP is tracking 2.5% for the year, supported by real wage growth of 1.8% and household net worth at record $156 trillion. Yet, we see early credit stress in unsecured lending, with charge-offs ticking up to 2.8% in credit cards, akin to what JPMorgan reported last quarter. In Europe (25% of revenue), growth is anemic at 1.1% amid fiscal austerity and energy transition costs; our CET1 ratio of 13.2% provides ample buffer against potential NPL rises, currently at 1.8% versus the Eurozone average of 2.4%. Asia-Pacific (15% revenue) offers tailwinds, with ex-China GDP at 4.6%; we're seeing 8% YoY loan growth in India and Southeast Asia via our digital platforms, mirroring HSBC's playbook. Latin America (5% revenue) faces headwinds from commodity volatility but strong remittance flows.

Translating this to our financials, the easing cycle poses NIM compression risks—we guide for a 5-10bps Q/Q decline in Q4 as deposit betas catch up (currently at 65% for non-interest-bearing deposits). That said, our loan-to-deposit ratio stands at a healthy 78%, with average loans up 7% YoY to $450 billion, led by 12% growth in commercial real estate (CRE) outside office sectors and 9% in mortgages. Fee income remains a bright spot, up 14% YoY to $2.1 billion, fueled by capital markets activity; our IB fees hit $850 million on M&A advisory, benefiting from $1.2 trillion in global deal volume YTD, though down 20% from peak 2021 levels.

Credit quality is stable but monitored closely. Provisions for credit losses (PCL) came in at $450 million in Q3, or 0.95% of loans, versus 1.05% guidance; we maintain a $3.2 billion ACL covering 2.1x annualized losses. Delinquencies are up 15bps QoQ to 1.2%, concentrated in auto loans (2.5%) amid affordability strains from 7.2% new auto rates. ROTE held at 11.8%, with EPS of $1.42 beating consensus by $0.05.

Strategic insights and technical initiatives underscore our proactive stance. First, deposit optimization: We've accelerated our high-yield savings push via the Apex Mobile app, growing core deposits 6% QoQ to $380 billion at a blended 2.1% cost—below peers like Wells Fargo's 2.4%. Second, digital transformation: Our AI-driven fraud detection, powered by machine learning models similar to those at Goldman Sachs' Marcus platform, reduced false positives by 30% and saved $120 million in losses YTD. We're also piloting blockchain-based tokenization for CRE loans, targeting $5 billion in assets by 2025 to enhance liquidity, in line with BlackRock's BUIDL fund momentum.

On ESG and sustainable finance, we've originated $15 billion in green loans YTD (up 25% YoY), including transition financing for European autos akin to BNP Paribas' offerings, capturing 150bps premia over vanilla lending. Risk management under Basel IV is robust; our standardized approach for IRB models keeps RWAs flat at $320 billion despite loan growth.

Forward-looking, we see 2025 global growth at 3.0%, with U.S. soft-landing odds at 65%. Downside risks include a 20% recession probability per our stress tests, which still deliver ROTE >10% and CET1 >11%. Upside from deregulation could boost IB fees 15-20%. We're guiding FY24 revenue growth of 6-7%, NIM 3.30-3.40%, and ROE 12%. Our $10 billion buyback authorization and 45bps dividend hike reflect confidence.

In summary, while macro headwinds test the sector—echoing the 2018-2019 rate cycle—our fortress balance sheet, tech edge, and geographic diversity enable outperformance.

Before we move on, I'd like to walk you through our full-year 2024 guidance, which we are affirming today at the midpoint, and then drill down into the key assumptions underpinning it. As a reminder, we're guiding to adjusted EPS of $4.85 to $5.05, representing 5% to 9% growth year-over-year; net interest income of $28.5 billion to $29.0 billion, up 3% at the midpoint; non-interest revenue of $18.0 billion to $18.5 billion; and a return on tangible common equity of 13% to 14%. Total expenses are expected to come in at $24.5 billion to $25.0 billion, reflecting our disciplined expense management amid ongoing investments.

Now, turning to the key assumptions underlying this guidance—these are critical guardrails that reflect our base case scenario, informed by our proprietary econometric models, consensus economist forecasts from sources like the Philadelphia Fed Survey of Professional Forecasters, and real-time data from our $1.2 trillion loan book and $900 billion deposit franchise. We'll assume no material deterioration in macroeconomic conditions beyond what's already priced in, and our guidance is contingent on these factors holding steady. Let me break it down by category for clarity.

First, the macroeconomic and interest rate environment. We're baking in U.S. real GDP growth of 2.3% to 2.6% for calendar 2024, aligning with the latest Blue Chip Economic Indicators consensus, with quarterly acceleration into Q4 driven by resilient consumer spending—household disposable income growth holding at 3.5% amid wage gains outpacing inflation. Unemployment stabilizes at 4.1% to 4.3%, per BLS projections. On the rate front, we assume the Fed funds rate remains in the 5.00% to 5.25% target range through year-end, with just 25 basis points of cuts in December, followed by another 50 bps in Q1 2025. This implies a flatter yield curve, with the 10-year Treasury yield averaging 4.1% to 4.3%—supportive of our net interest margin stabilizing at 3.45% to 3.55%. Our asset-sensitive balance sheet, with 62% of loans variable-rate or repricing within 12 months, positions us well here, though we're monitoring SOFR-linked loan demand closely. Globally, we assume ECB rates peak at 4.25% with cuts starting Q4, and modest BOE easing, which underpins our 4% cross-border loan growth ex-U.S.

Second, balance sheet growth dynamics. Loan balances are projected to expand 4% to 5% year-over-year to $1.25 trillion, weighted toward high-quality C&I lending at 6% growth—fueled by middle-market deal flow in healthcare and tech sectors, where we've seen pipeline strength via our relationships with PE firms like Blackstone and KKR. Consumer loans grow modestly at 2%, anchored by auto and credit card originations, assuming auto ABS spreads hold at 250-300 bps over Treasuries. Mortgage warehouse lines moderate to 3% growth post the refi boom. Deposits remain our funding bedrock, growing 3% to $950 billion, with core transaction accounts at 70% of mix; we assume beta compression to 65% on interest-bearing deposits as competition eases from the likes of regional players post-SVB fallout. Wholesale funding costs stay capped at LIBOR+75 bps via our strong access to the FHLB window and term repo markets.

Credit quality assumptions are conservative but constructive. Under CECL, we expect provision expense of $2.8 billion to $3.0 billion, or 85-90 bps of loans, with net charge-offs ticking up to 45 bps from 38 bps in Q2—primarily in unsecured consumer, where delinquencies rise to 2.8% from 2.4%, reflecting credit normalization but still below 2019 troughs. Commercial migration to criticized/special mention stays flat at 1.8%, supported by our 55% loan-to-value on CRE office exposure, which we continue to underweight versus peers. Office CRE net charge-offs assumed at 75 bps on that $40 billion book, with no exposure to high-risk urban trophy assets. Our ALLL coverage ratio holds at 1.25x annualized charge-offs, providing a $4 billion buffer.

Non-interest revenue drivers hinge on market volatility and strategic ramps. Fee income grows 6% to $17.2 billion, led by capital markets with investment banking fees up 10% on M&A rebound—our advisory backlog is up 15% QoQ, targeting $1.2 billion in fees from deals like the rumored healthcare roll-ups. Trading revenue assumes VIX averaging 18, delivering $2.4 billion, flat YoY. Payments and cards grow 8% via our Visa/Mastercard interchange normalization post-reg caps, and treasury management wins with corporates migrating to our RTP-enabled platform. Wealth management AUM expands 7% to $450 billion on 5% market appreciation—S&P 500 to 5,600—plus 2% organic flows into ESG and alternatives products, where we've launched three new interval funds co-branded with BlackRock.

Expense discipline amid tech transformation. Our efficiency ratio targets 56% to 57%, with expenses up only 2% excluding FDIC special assessment residuals. This embeds $800 million in run-rate savings from our Horizon 3.0 initiative—cloud migration to AWS for 40% of core banking stack, reducing data center TCO by 25%; AI-driven fraud detection cutting false positives 30% via our partnership with Feedzai; and robotic process automation for 20% of back-office ops. Regulatory costs, including Basel III Endgame final rules, add $150 million—we're positioning our CET1 ratio at 11.2% to 11.5%, well above our 10.5% target and compliant with Category II stress test scenarios projecting HQLA at 145% of requirements.

Regionally, U.S. operations drive 85% of earnings with 5% NII growth; Europe flatlines at 2% amid slower ECB cuts but bolstered by our €50 billion ESG-linked green loan book, up 12% YoY in line with EU Taxonomy demand; Asia-Pacific accelerates to 8% revenue growth via digital consumer banking expansion in India and Southeast Asia, where our UPI interoperability with PhonePe has onboarded 2 million new wallets. Strategically, we're assuming continued fintech collaboration—no outright disruption—with integrations like Plaid for open banking APIs driving 15% deposit inflows from millennials, and our blockchain-based trade finance pilot with IBM scaling to $5 billion in volume.

These assumptions represent our modal scenario as of today, with sensitivity analysis showing EPS resilient to +50 bps Fed pause or -25 bps GDP shock. We're not guiding recession probability above 20%, per our models, but our fortress balance sheet—liquidity coverage ratio at 125%, tangible book value $42 per share—gives us optionality. We'll update with Q4 results next quarter.

Turning now to our deposit franchise, which remains a cornerstone of our balance sheet strength and a key driver of our net interest margin expansion. In this higher-for-longer rate environment—with the Fed funds rate hovering around 5.25% to 5.50%—deposit dynamics have been fluid, influenced by elevated Treasury yields pulling customers toward money market funds and direct issuance platforms like those from TreasuryDirect or fintech disruptors such as Ally and SoFi. Despite these headwinds, we delivered robust deposit growth of 9.2% year-over-year, or $13.8 billion, bringing total deposits to $158.4 billion as of quarter-end. This outpaced the industry average of 6.1% per the latest FDIC call report data and compares favorably to peers like Regions Financial and Fifth Third, who reported mid-single-digit growth.

Let me break this down by deposit mix—transactional, savings, and time deposits—to highlight the trends and our proactive strategies.

Transactional deposits, which include our demand deposit accounts, or DDAs, and NOW accounts, represent 42% of our total mix, down slightly from 45% a year ago but stable sequentially. We saw 4.8% YoY growth here, adding $2.1 billion to reach $66.6 billion. Non-interest-bearing DDAs, our lowest-cost funding source at just 12 basis points in Q2, grew modestly by 2.9% YoY to $38.2 billion, reflecting some modest outflows from commercial clients optimizing liquidity amid inverted yield curves. Consumer checking balances held firm, bolstered by our embedded finance partnerships with payroll providers like ADP.

Regionally, the Southeast—our core franchise spanning Florida, Georgia, and the Carolinas—drove 60% of this growth, with transactional deposits up 7% YoY, fueled by small business inflows from our expanded Treasury Management suite, including same-day ACH and RTP capabilities via The Clearing House network. In contrast, our Northeast markets, like New York and Boston, experienced flat growth due to intense competition from digital banks and money center peers like JPMorgan Chase, where corporate treasury shifts to sweep accounts have pressured low-cost deposits industry-wide.

Savings deposits, encompassing consumer and commercial savings accounts, money market deposit accounts, or MMDAs, and high-yield online savings, now comprise 38% of the mix, up from 35% YoY, and grew a strong 14.1% or $6.4 billion to $51.8 billion. Average rates paid here ticked up to 3.85% from 2.9% a year ago—our deposit beta remains disciplined at 45%—but these remain core, relationship-driven funds with betas below those of time deposits.

Key trend: A pronounced shift from transactional to savings as consumers chase yield, with MMDA balances surging 18% YoY amid 5%+ APYs on short-term Treasuries. Our "Apex Yield Saver" product, launched last quarter with tiered rates up to 4.75% for balances over $250,000 linked to direct deposit, captured $2.3 billion in new inflows, primarily from digital channels. This mirrors industry patterns seen at Wells Fargo and PNC, where promotional savings have offset DDA erosion.

Strategically, we've layered in technical initiatives like AI-driven personalization via our mobile app—using machine learning models trained on transaction data to recommend yield ladders—and expanded our "Deposit Boost" program, offering 25 bps rate bumps for clients bundling with our wealth management arms. In the Midwest expansion markets, like Ohio and Michigan, savings growth hit 20% YoY, outpacing our LDR compression goals and supporting a loan-to-deposit ratio of 82%, down 150 bps from last year.

Time deposits, including retail CDs, jumbo CDs, and brokered deposits, make up the remaining 20% of our mix at $31.9 billion, up 12.7% YoY or $3.6 billion. While this category grew fastest, average rates rose to 4.62%, reflecting competitive brokered CD pricing via platforms like IntraFi Network. Retail CDs, at 65% of this bucket, expanded 10% with our "Lock & Grow" 12-month specials at 5.00% APY, attracting $1.8 billion from rate-sensitive seniors in Florida retirement communities.

We've been deliberate here, capping brokered at 8% of total deposits—well below the 15% regulatory watch level—to prioritize sticky core deposits. Trends show time deposits repricing faster, with a 60% beta, but they've stabilized our funding costs amid wholesale borrowing spikes; FHLB advances declined 22% QoQ as a result.

Our deposit strategy centers on mix optimization: growing low-beta core deposits (under 3.50% rates) to 85% of total from 82%, targeting a 25 bps NIM accretion in the second half. Initiatives include: digital acquisition with 35% of new deposits via app/web, with QR-code branch deposits and Zelle integration boosting transactional stickiness; relationship pricing dynamic tiers via our core banking system rewarding multi-product households with 50 bps premiums; regional tailwinds with $500 million allocated to Southeast branch remodels with deposit-gathering ATMs; hedging Midwest growth via mBridge cross-border corridors for commercial inflows; and risk mitigation stress-tested for 100 bps rate cuts, with $10 billion in excess liquidity to avoid outflow flights like those hitting SVB in '23.

Looking ahead, we expect 7-9% full-year deposit growth, with transactional stabilizing and savings moderating as rates peak. This positions us for 3.65-3.75% NIM in Q4, ahead of peers. Our C-suite deposit war room, meeting bi-weekly, ensures agility against fintech threats and recessionary drawdowns.

I'll now address our deposit funding dynamics, specifically the cost of deposits, where we saw some predictable upward pressure in the quarter amid sustained elevated rates and intensifying competition. Our total deposit costs averaged 2.85% in Q2, up 25 basis points quarter-over-quarter from 2.60% in Q1 and 110 basis points year-over-year from 1.75% in Q2 2023. This reflects a deposit beta of approximately 45% on the Fed's cumulative 525 basis point hiking cycle since March 2022, which is tracking at the lower end of our peer group—think JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America, who are reporting betas closer to 55-60% due to their heavier reliance on brokered and time deposits.

Breaking this down by deposit category: our core non-interest-bearing demand deposits, which make up 28% of our total $145 billion average deposit base, held steady at a near-zero cost of just 0.15%, benefiting from our strong commercial relationship banking franchise. However, interest-bearing deposits drove the lift: savings and NOW accounts climbed to 2.40% from 2.10%, while money market deposit accounts (MMDAs) and consumer CDs rose to 3.25% and 4.10%, respectively. Time deposit costs were the biggest mover at 4.55%, up from 4.20%, as we selectively priced specials to retain high-value municipal and commercial relationships amid outflows.

The environment remains frothy, with deposit betas repricing faster than we've seen in prior cycles. National players like Ally Bank and SoFi are aggressively marketing high-yield savings accounts at 4.50-5.00%, siphoning retail liquidity—our consumer deposit outflows were $1.2 billion in Q2, modest but concentrated in the under-$250k segment. Money market funds yielding 5.20-5.40% continue to compete vigorously, per ICI data showing $200 billion in net inflows YTD, while short-term Treasury bills at 5.30% add tailwinds to disintermediation risks. Regionally, this varies: in our Southeast franchise (Florida and Georgia markets, 35% of deposits), competitive intensity is acute from fintechs and credit unions offering promotional CDs north of 4.75%, pushing our local beta to 50%. Conversely, our Midwest core (Illinois, Ohio) saw more stable dynamics, with average costs at 2.65% thanks to sticky commercial deposits from manufacturing and agribusiness clients less sensitive to rate shopping.

We've also monitored the regional banking fallout post-SVB and Signature—while our uninsured deposits stand at 22% (down from 25% pre-March 2023 via proactive diversification), we've seen tactical shifts where depositors favor "too-big-to-fail" names, indirectly pressuring mid-caps like ours on pricing.

To mitigate, we've layered in several initiatives. First, our dynamic pricing engine—enhanced with AI-driven deposit beta forecasting tied to FOMC projections and Treasury curves—allowed us to cap promotional CD rates at 4.25% for 95% of new issuance, versus market at 4.60%. This preserved a 35 bps spread advantage over peers. Second, we accelerated our "Deposit Shield" program, blending relationship incentives like fee waivers and embedded lending perks, which boosted core deposit growth by 2.1% QoQ in commercial banking. On the tech front, our mobile app's real-time yield comparator tool, rolled out Q1, has reduced churn by 15% among digital natives by transparently showing our competitive positioning net of service value.

Strategically, we're shifting mix: non-interest-bearing deposits grew 4% QoQ to $40.6 billion, targeting a 30% mix by year-end through C-suite treasury management wins. We're also de-emphasizing brokered CDs (now <5% of funding) in favor of reciprocal deposits via networks like IntraFi, which added $800 million at a blended 3.80% cost—cheaper than FHLB advances now pricing at 5.40%. This keeps our loan-to-deposit ratio at a pristine 82%, insulating NIM at 3.45% (down just 8 bps QoQ).

Looking ahead, we expect Q3 deposit costs to rise another 10-15 bps to 2.95-3.00%, assuming steady Fed funds at 5.25-5.50%. If cuts materialize in September as futures imply (75% probability per CME FedWatch), our lagged beta should stabilize costs mid-3s by Q4 2025. Competitively, we'll lean into our 4.2% household penetration in key MSAs and expand our BaaS partnerships with fintechs like Chime for low-cost flow deposits. Risks include a steeper yield curve inversion reigniting outflows, but our $15 billion liquidity buffer and diversified wholesale funding position us resiliently.

Overall, deposit costs are manageable and below our long-term 3.25% target, supporting 12-14% ROTE.

As we dive into the fee income segment, which remains a cornerstone of our diversified revenue model, total non-interest income from fees reached $2.8 billion in the quarter, up 14% year-over-year and 5% quarter-over-quarter. This marks our strongest fee performance since Q4 2022, driven by resilient client activity across our core franchises amid a backdrop of moderating inflation, steady equity markets – with the S&P 500 up 8% YTD – and a pickup in M&A volumes globally.

Excluding one-time items like the $150 million in advisory mandates from last year's restructuring wave, our core fee income grew 12% YoY, underscoring the durability of our business model. Fees now represent 28% of our total revenue, up from 25% a year ago, as we continue to de-risk our balance sheet from net interest income volatility. Let me break this down by our three primary fee pillars: wealth management, investment banking, and cards, highlighting key performance drivers, regional nuances, and the technical initiatives fueling growth.

Wealth management delivered another standout quarter, with fees hitting $1.35 billion, a 16% YoY increase and representing 48% of our total fee pool – our largest contributor. This was propelled by a 12% rise in average assets under management, or AUM, to $1.9 trillion, benefiting from both net new money inflows of $45 billion – our best since the post-pandemic rebound – and favorable market tailwinds. Advisory and asset-based fees, which make up 65% of this segment, grew 18% YoY, while performance fees ticked up 5% to $120 million on the back of strong alternatives performance.

Key drivers included heightened demand for our high-margin alternatives platform, where private credit and infrastructure funds saw $18 billion in inflows, capturing share from pure-play managers like Blackstone and KKR amid yields compressing to 7-9% from 10%+ peaks. Our ESG and sustainable investing suite, now 22% of AUM, grew 25% YoY, aligning with regulatory tailwinds like the EU's SFDR and client mandates from sovereign wealth funds in the Middle East.

Regionally, the Americas drove 55% of growth, with ultra-high-net-worth client acquisition in our model adding 150,000 relationships. APAC was the star, up 28% YoY on $12 billion inflows from Greater China HNWIs rotating into our offshore platforms amid domestic market volatility – think Hang Seng down 5% YTD. EMEA faced headwinds from UK client outflows tied to pension fund de-risking, but our continental Europe franchise offset this with 10% growth via partnerships with family offices in Switzerland and Germany.

Technically, our "Wealth360" digital advisor platform, powered by GenAI for personalized portfolio construction, boosted client retention to 96% and cross-sell ratios to 3.2 products per client – up from 2.8. We've embedded predictive analytics to flag life-event triggers, like inheritance planning, driving a 20% uptick in annuity and trust fees. Strategically, we're targeting 15-18% annual fee growth through 2026 by scaling our $500 million investment in Model Wealth Portfolios with active overlays for alpha generation.

Shifting to investment banking, fees came in at $900 million, surging 22% YoY and 8% sequentially – our highest since Q1 2021's SPAC frenzy. This reflects a broad-based recovery in league tables, where we climbed to #4 globally in advisory per Dealogic, behind only Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan, and Morgan Stanley. M&A advisory, 55% of IB fees, exploded 35% YoY to $495 million, fueled by $250 billion in announced deals, including our role in the $45 billion activist-led takeover of a Big Tech peer reminiscent of Elliott's push on Twitter.

ECM and DCM underwriting added $280 million, up 15% YoY, with IPO pipelines firming on lower volatility – VIX averaging 14 vs. 20+ last year. Our sweet spot remains mid-cap tech and healthcare, where we priced 12 follow-ons at tight spreads, averaging 2.5% fees. Leveraged finance syndication contributed $125 million, steady despite high rates, as we originated $30 billion in high-yield paper for private equity sponsors like Apollo.

Regionally, APAC led with 30% YoY growth on cross-border deals into India and Southeast Asia – e.g., advising on a $10 billion fintech merger akin to Grab-Uber talks. The Americas held 60% share, buoyed by U.S. mega-deals, while EMEA lagged at +5% due to antitrust scrutiny in energy transitions, though our London hub captured Brexit-related restructurings.

Operationally, our IB tech stack – including Symphony for deal collaboration and our proprietary "AlphaFlow" AI for pitchbook generation – reduced cycle times by 25%, enabling us to win 18% more mandates. We're leaning into blockchain for settlement via pilots with DTCC, cutting T+2 to T+1. Outlook-wise, with M&A multiples stabilizing at 10-12x EBITDA and $2 trillion in dry powder, we see IB fees growing 20%+ in the second half, assuming no recession.

Rounding out the breakdown, cards and payments generated $550 million in fees, up 8% YoY – resilient in a high-rate environment where consumer spending grew just 3% per Census data. Interchange and network fees, 70% of this bucket, rose 10% to $385 million on 12% transaction volume growth to 450 million swipes, driven by our premium Visa Signature and Mastercard World Elite co-brand partnerships with airlines like Delta and retailers like Amazon.

Annual fees and rewards rebates added $110 million, up 6%, as we migrated 2 million clients to our no-fee cashback tiers, boosting usage rates to 85%. Merchant acquiring, via our platform, contributed $55 million, flat YoY amid pricing pressure but with upside from SMB digital adoption.

U.S. volumes dominated at 65%, with travel rebound – think 15% growth in cross-border – offsetting slowdowns in discretionary retail. APAC grew 18% on our WeChat Pay integration in China and UPI linkages in India, adding 5 million wallets. EMEA saw 4% growth, tempered by PSD2 open banking regs forcing fee compression.

Key initiatives include our "PaySmart" tokenization engine, leveraging Apple Pay and Google Wallet for 30% faster authorizations and fraud rates down to 0.05%. We've rolled out BNPL features with partners, driving 25% uptake among Gen Z. Strategically, cross-selling cards into wealth clients lifted attachment rates to 45%, and we're eyeing 10-12% CAGR through embedded finance in our corporate banking app, targeting $1 billion in fees by 2027.

In aggregate, these franchises benefited from a 22% increase in active client relationships to 45 million, with cross-sell synergies adding 200 basis points to fee margins. Our focus on fee diversification – now 60% recurring – shields us from NII compression as Fed funds hold at 5.25-5.50%. Risks include geopolitical tensions curbing APAC M&A and potential equity derating, but our $300 million in tech capex positions us for outperformance.

Looking forward, we guide to mid-teens fee growth for FY2024, with wealth and IB as accelerants. We're excited about Q4 catalysts like earnings-driven ECM and our alternatives roadshow.

Finally, turning to our credit quality metrics, which continue to reflect the resilience of our well-underwritten portfolios amid a dynamic macroeconomic environment. Our disciplined origination standards, proactive risk management, and targeted portfolio optimization initiatives have positioned us favorably as we navigate elevated interest rates, persistent inflation, and sector-specific headwinds like those in commercial real estate (CRE) and auto lending. Let me walk you through the key trends in non-performing loans (NPLs), charge-offs, and delinquencies, with segment and regional breakdowns, before sharing our forward-looking analysis.

Starting with the headline numbers for Q3 2024: Our net charge-off (NCO) ratio came in at 52 basis points (bps), down 8 bps quarter-over-quarter (QoQ) from 60 bps in Q2 and flat year-over-year (YoY) versus 52 bps in Q3 2023. This marks our lowest quarterly NCO since Q4 2021, driven by stabilization in consumer credit cards and commercial loans.

The NPL ratio (loans 90+ days past due or on non-accrual, excluding government-guaranteed loans) improved to 92 bps, a 5 bps decline QoQ from 97 bps and a robust 25 bps improvement YoY from 117 bps. Excluding our CRE office portfolio, the core NPL ratio is even stronger at 78 bps.

Delinquency rates showed modest sequential pressure: 30-89 days past due rose to 1.85% from 1.72% in Q2, but remain down 15 bps YoY from 2.00%. Early-stage delinquencies (30+ days) ticked up to 2.42%, reflecting seasonal patterns and higher payment shocks from the Fed's cumulative 525 bps of rate hikes since 2022.

These metrics compare favorably to industry peers. In consumer lending (45% of portfolio, $28B outstanding): NCOs improved sharply to 1.12%, down from 1.35% QoQ, led by credit cards (1.85% NCO vs. 2.10% prior) where our vintage analysis shows 2022-2023 originations performing 25% better than pre-pandemic cohorts due to our AI-enhanced underwriting models, which now incorporate alternative data like cash flow volatility from Plaid integrations. In commercial & industrial (C&I) and CRE (40% of portfolio, $25B outstanding): NCOs compressed to 18 bps from 28 bps QoQ, with NPLs at 1.45% (down from 1.62%). C&I delinquencies are pristine at 0.45%, supported by our middle-market focus on recession-resistant sectors like healthcare and tech services.

Government guaranteed (15% of portfolio, primarily SBA 7(a) loans): NPLs negligible at 0.12%, with zero charge-offs—our participation in the SBA's EIDL forgiveness program continues to yield attractive risk-adjusted returns.

Regionally: U.S. Southeast and Midwest (65% of loans): Credit quality is pristine—NPLs at 75 bps, delinquencies at 1.65%. Low unemployment (3.2% regional average vs. 4.1% national) and our granular local underwriting have buffered against national trends. Southwest (20%): Modest pressure in energy-exposed C&I, with NCOs at 65 bps, but mitigated by hedging mandates in our oil & gas book. International (15%, via our European branch network): NPLs stable at 1.20%, outperforming Eurozone banks (ECB median 1.85%) thanks to our focus on AAA-rated sovereigns and blue-chip corporates. UK delinquencies rose 10 bps to 1.95% amid Brexit-related supply chain echoes, but our stress testing under Basel III shows ample headroom.

We've accelerated several initiatives post-CECL adoption: Advanced Analytics Platform rolled out GenAI-powered early warning systems (in partnership with FIS) that flag 30+ delinquencies 45 days earlier, reducing NCOs by 15% in pilot segments through automated workout offers. Portfolio Optimization: Executed $1.2B in non-strategic sales (avg. yield 4.2%), lowering criticized and classified loans to 2.1% from 2.8% YoY. Collections Enhancement: 20% staff augmentation in our digital collections hub, achieving 85% cure rates on 60-day delinquencies via omnichannel (app, SMS, IVR) strategies—outpacing industry benchmarks from TransUnion.

Provision for Credit Losses (PCL) expense was $145M, or 35 bps of average loans, below our Q2 $162M as economic forecasts stabilized (GDP nowcast +2.1% from +1.8%). Our ACL stands at 1.45% of loans ($1.15B), with 155% coverage of NPLs and 2.8x projected NCOs over the next four quarters. CECL reserve releases of $20M reflect improving loss rates on 2021-2023 vintages.

Credit quality remains our north star, with macro tailwinds from potential Fed pauses outweighing near-term consumer stress. We expect Q4 NCOs of 45-55 bps, NPLs of 85-95 bps, and delinquencies stabilizing at 1.8-2.0%. Longer-term, we're targeting sub-50 bps NCOs by 2025 through further diversification away from rate-sensitive autos/CRE (target <30% exposure), scaling our "Horizon Score" proprietary model blending machine learning with macroeconomic overlays (e.g., unemployment, CPI proxies), and opportunistic M&A in high-quality consumer banks to accretively grow low-NPL portfolios.

In summary, our metrics underscore a fortress balance sheet, with proactive management turning headwinds into opportunities.
